changes.after: Understand why one text symbol can use two char units.

before: A char stores one 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. Single quotes such as 'A' create a char literal; double quotes create a String.
Some Unicode code points need a surrogate pair: two char units. String.length counts UTF-16 units, not necessarily complete code points or visible graphemes.
String.codePointCount(begin, end) counts code points in that range of char indexes. End is exclusive. This is still not a complete count of user-perceived graphemes.
The smiley in this example is written with two Unicode escapes, \uD83D and \uDE00, representing its surrogate pair. Its length is two while its code-point count is one.

Expected output or behavior: 2
1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare the two measurements for A and the supplied smiley. Do not label either measurement a universal count of visible symbols. You may trace it without a JDK; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: UTF-16 is Java's way of storing text as numbered units. A char holds one such unit. Single quotes make a char value; double quotes make a String, which can hold many units.
Unicode gives text elements numbers called code points. Some code points need two UTF-16 units. Those two units together are called a surrogate pair.

String.length counts UTF-16 units. codePointCount counts code points between two positions: it includes the start and stops before the end. Neither always counts the symbols a reader sees, because one visible symbol can combine code points.
The example stores one smiley using two Unicode escapes. An escape writes a text unit using its number instead of showing the symbol directly. The two escapes here form one surrogate pair.
The program prints 2, then 1 on the next line. The smiley uses two UTF-16 units but is one code point.
The letter A needs only one UTF-16 unit. The quiz asks what both measurements show when it replaces the smiley.

before.question: Replace the symbol string with "A". What do the measurements show?
choices: 1 and 2 because code points always outnumber char units.
1 and 1 because this letter occupies one UTF-16 unit and one code point.
before.explanation: A uses one code unit, unlike the supplementary smiley’s surrogate pair.

after.question: Replace the symbol string with "A". What prints?
choices: 2 then 1, because all strings have those counts.
1 then 2, because code points always outnumber units.
1 then 1, because A uses one unit and one code point.
after.explanation: A fits in one UTF-16 unit and is one code point, so both counts are one.
